problems.problem: Paul and Jenny each have a whole number of pounds. Paul says to Jenny: if you give me £3, I will have $n$ times as much as you. Jenny says to Paul: if you give me £$n$, I will have 3 times as much as you. Given that both statements are true and $n$ is a positive integer, find all possible values of $n$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle, and let $D$, $E$ be the feet of the perpendiculars from $A$, $B$ onto $BC$, $CA$ respectively. Let $P$ be the point where line $AD$ meets the semicircle drawn outwardly on $BC$, and let $Q$ be the point where line $BE$ meets the semicircle drawn outwardly on $AC$. Prove that $CP = CQ$.

Find the smallest natural number $n$ such that, however the elements of $\{1,2,\dots,n\}$ are coloured red or blue, there always exist integers $x,y,z,w$ in the set, of the same colour and not necessarily distinct, with $x+y+z=w$.
Find the least possible value of the largest term of an arithmetic progression consisting of seven distinct prime numbers.

Let $S$ be a set of rational numbers such that (i) $\tfrac12 \in S$, and (ii) whenever $x \in S$, both $\tfrac{1}{x+1} \in S$ and $\tfrac{x}{x+1} \in S$. Prove that $S$ contains every rational number strictly between 0 and 1.
Let $n$ be an integer greater than 6. Prove that if $n-1$ and $n+1$ are both prime, then $n^2(n^2+16)$ is divisible by 720. Is the converse true?

A teacher has a class of six pairs of twins and wants to form quiz teams so that no pair of twins is ever placed on the same team. Subject to this condition: (i) in how many ways can the class be split into two teams of six, and (ii) in how many ways can it be split into three teams of four?
In cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$, diagonal $AC$ bisects angle $DAB$. Side $AD$ is extended beyond $D$ to a point $E$. Show that $CE = CA$ if and only if $DE = AB$.

An equilateral triangle $ABC$ with integer side length $N$ is divided by lines parallel to its sides into unit equilateral cells. A continuous route starts inside the cell containing vertex $A$ and always passes from one cell to an adjacent one through a shared edge, never visiting any cell twice. Find, with proof, the greatest possible number of cells visited.
Let $G$ be a convex quadrilateral. Show that there exists a point $X$ in the plane such that every line through $X$ divides $G$ into two regions of equal area, if and only if $G$ is a parallelogram.
Let $T$ be a set of 2005 points in the plane, no three collinear. Show that, for any point of $T$, the number of triangles (with vertices in $T$) that strictly contain that point is even.
Find four prime numbers less than 100 that divide $3^{32} - 2^{32}$.

In convex quadrilateral $ABCD$, points $M,N$ lie on side $AB$ with $AM=MN=NB$, and points $P,Q$ lie on side $CD$ with $CP=PQ=QD$. Prove that the area of $AMCP$, the area of $MNPQ$, and $\tfrac13$ of the area of $ABCD$ are all equal.

The number 916238457 is a nine-digit number using each digit 1 to 9 exactly once, in which the digits 1-5 appear in increasing order but the digits 1-6 do not. How many nine-digit numbers with all distinct digits 1-9 have this same property?

Two circles $S$ and $T$ touch each other and share a common tangent line meeting $S$ at $A$ and $T$ at $B$. Let $AP$ be a diameter of $S$, and let the tangent from $P$ to $T$ touch $T$ at $Q$. Show that $AP = PQ$.
For positive real numbers $a,b,c$, prove that $(a^2+b^2)^2 \ge (a+b+c)(a+b-c)(b+c-a)(c+a-b)$.
Let $n$ be an integer. Show that if $2 + 2\sqrt{1+12n^2}$ is an integer, then it is a perfect square.
Find all positive integer solutions $x,y,z$ of the simultaneous equations $x+y-z=12$ and $x^2+y^2-z^2=12$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with an obtuse angle at $A$. Let $Q$ be a point on the circumcircle of $ABC$, different from $A$, $B$, $C$, on the same side of chord $BC$ as $A$, and let $P$ be the other end of the diameter through $Q$. Let $V$, $W$ be the feet of the perpendiculars from $Q$ onto $CA$, $AB$ respectively. Prove that triangles $PBC$ and $AWV$ are similar.
Let $S$ be a 756-element subset of $\{1,2,\dots,2008\}$. Show that $S$ contains two distinct elements $a,b$ such that $a+b$ is divisible by 8.

Let $P$ be an interior point of triangle $ABC$. The line through $P$ parallel to $AB$ meets $BC$ at $L$; the line through $P$ parallel to $BC$ meets $CA$ at $M$; the line through $P$ parallel to $CA$ meets $AB$ at $N$. Prove that $\dfrac{BL}{LC}\cdot\dfrac{CM}{MA}\cdot\dfrac{AN}{NB} \le \dfrac18$, and determine the position of $P$ for which equality holds.

The function $f$ on the positive integers satisfies $f(1)=1$, $f(2n)=2f(n)$, and $n f(2n+1) = (2n+1)(f(n)+n)$ for all $n \ge 1$. (i) Prove that $f(n)$ is always an integer. (ii) For how many positive integers less than 2007 does $f(n)=2n$?
On a standard 8x8 chessboard, a zig-zag path is a set of eight white squares, one in each row, each pair in consecutive rows meeting at a corner. How many zig-zag paths are there?
Find all real numbers $x,y,z$ satisfying $(x+1)yz=12$, $(y+1)zx=4$, and $(z+1)xy=4$.
Let $ABPC$ be a parallelogram such that triangle $ABC$ is acute-angled. The circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ meets line $CP$ again at $Q$. Prove that $PQ = AC$ if and only if angle $BAC = 60^\circ$.
Find all positive integers $n$ such that $n+2008$ divides $n^2+2008$ and $n+2009$ divides $n^2+2009$.
Determine all sequences $a_0,a_1,a_2,\dots$ satisfying $a_{n+1}=2a_n^2-1$ for every $n \ge 0$, with $a_0$ rational, such that $a_i=a_j$ for some $i \ne j$.
Obtuse triangle $ABC$ has sides $a,b,c$ opposite angles $A,B,C$ respectively. Prove that $a^3\cos A + b^3\cos B + c^3\cos C < abc$.
Find all integers $x,y,z$ such that $x^2+y^2+z^2 = 2(yz+1)$ and $x+y+z=4018$.
Points $A,B,C,D,E$ lie in that order on a circle, with lines $AB$ and $ED$ parallel. Prove that angle $ABC = 90^\circ$ if and only if $AC^2 = BD^2 + CE^2$.

Isaac attempts all six questions of an Olympiad paper in order, each marked from 0 to 10, and never scores more on a later question than on any earlier one. How many different sequences of six marks can he achieve?

Two circles of different radii, centred at $B$ and $C$, touch externally at $A$. A common tangent not through $A$ touches the first circle at $D$ and the second at $E$. The line through $A$ perpendicular to $DE$ meets the perpendicular bisector of $BC$ at $F$. Prove that $BC = 2AF$.
Find all real-valued functions $f$ on the reals satisfying $f(x)f(y) = f(x+y) + xy$ for all real $x,y$.
Treasure is buried at an integer point $(x,y)$. A map shows the values of $x^2+y$ and $x+y^2$, which are distinct numbers. Prove that these two values determine $(x,y)$ uniquely.
One integer is removed from the set $\{1,2,\dots,n\}$. The average of the remaining numbers is $40\tfrac{3}{4}$. Which integer was removed?

Let $s$ be an integer greater than 6. A solid cube of side $s$ has a square hole of side $x<6$ drilled straight through between opposite faces. The volume of the remaining solid equals, numerically, its total surface area. Find all possible integer values of $x$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle right-angled at $A$, and let $L$ lie on side $BC$ between $B$ and $C$. The circle through $A,B,L$ meets line $AC$ again at $M$, and the circle through $C,A,L$ meets line $AB$ again at $N$. Prove that $L,M,N$ are collinear.

Each of the 64 unit squares of a chessboard is coloured red, white, or blue; a coloured pattern is called an arrangement. Determine whether more arrangements contain an even number of red squares or more contain an odd number of red squares.

Circles $S_1$ and $S_2$ meet at $L$ and $M$. Let $P$ be a point on $S_2$; let lines $PL$ and $PM$ meet $S_1$ again at $Q$ and $R$ respectively, and let lines $QM$ and $RL$ meet at $K$. Show that, as $P$ varies on $S_2$, $K$ traces a fixed circle.
Let $a,b,c$ be the side lengths of a triangle with $ab+bc+ca=1$. Show that $(a+1)(b+1)(c+1) < 4$.
Find all integers $n$ (positive or negative) for which $n^2+20n+11$ is a perfect square, justifying that all values have been found.
For the numbers $1,2,\dots,n$, find, in terms of $n$, the largest integer $t$ such that they can be arranged in a row so that every pair of consecutive terms differs by at least $t$.

A point $P$ lies outside a circle $S$, and a line through $P$ meets $S$ at distinct points $X,Y$. Circles $S_1,S_2$ pass through $P$ and are tangent to $S$ at $X,Y$ respectively. Prove that the difference of the radii of $S_1$ and $S_2$ does not depend on the choice of $P,X,Y$.

Two bags contain $m$ and $n$ balls respectively ($m,n>0$). Two operations are allowed: (a) remove an equal number of balls from each bag; (b) double the number of balls in one bag. Is it always possible to empty both bags in finitely many operations? If operation (b) is replaced by tripling the balls in one bag, is it still always possible?
Prove that the product of four consecutive positive integers can never equal the product of two consecutive positive integers.
Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with feet of altitudes $D$ (from $A$), $E$ (from $B$), $F$ (from $C$). Prove that $DE+DF \le BC$, and determine when equality holds.

Counters are placed on an 8 by 8 chessboard, at most one per square. Determine the maximum number that can be placed so that no row, no column, and neither of the two main diagonals contains five or more counters.
Circles $S$ and $T$ touch at $X$ and share a common tangent meeting $S$ at $A$ and $T$ at distinct point $B$. Let $AP$ be a diameter of $S$. Prove that $B$, $X$, $P$ are collinear.
Find all real $x,y,z$ satisfying $x^2-4y+7=0$, $y^2-6z+14=0$, $z^2-2x-7=0$ simultaneously.
Find all positive integers $n$ such that $12n-119$ and $75n-539$ are both perfect squares.
A triangle has side lengths at most 2, 3, and 4 respectively. Determine, with proof, its maximum possible area.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle. Let $S$ be the circle through $B$ tangent to $CA$ at $A$, and $T$ the circle through $C$ tangent to $AB$ at $A$; $S$ and $T$ meet again at $D$. Let $E$ be the second intersection of line $AD$ with the circumcircle of $ABC$. Prove that $D$ is the midpoint of $AE$.

In acute triangle $ABC$, $E$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $B$ to $CA$. Let $\ell$ be the tangent to the circumcircle of $ABC$ at $B$, and let $F$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $C$ to $\ell$. Prove that $EF$ is parallel to $AB$.
A number, written in base 10, consists of $3^{2013}$ copies of the digit 3 and no other digit. Find the highest power of 3 dividing this number.
Over a nine-day holiday, Isaac does exactly one of surfing, water-skiing, or resting each day, and never does the two different water-sports on consecutive days. How many schedules are possible?

Let $ABC$ be equilateral and $P$ an interior point, with $D,E,F$ the feet of the perpendiculars from $P$ to $BC,CA,AB$ respectively. Prove (a) $AF+BD+CE = AE+BF+CD$, and (b) area($APF$)+area($BPD$)+area($CPE$) = area($APE$)+area($BPF$)+area($CPD$).
A triangle has angles $A,B,C$ (in degrees) and opposite sides $a,b,c$. Prove that $60 \le \dfrac{aA+bB+cC}{a+b+c} < 90$.
Order the numbers $3^{3^4}$, $3^{4^3}$, $3^{4^4}$, $4^{3^3}$, $4^{3^4}$ from smallest to largest, justifying the order (here $a^{b^c}$ means $a^{(b^c)}$).
Positive integers $p,a,b$ satisfy $p^2+a^2=b^2$. Prove that if $p$ is a prime greater than 3, then $a$ is a multiple of 12 and $2(p+a+1)$ is a perfect square.
A hotel has ten rooms on each side of a corridor. A team leader wants to book seven rooms so that no two booked rooms on the same side of the corridor are adjacent. In how many ways can this be done?
Let $x$ be real with $t = x + x^{-1}$ an integer greater than 2. Prove that $t_n = x^n + x^{-n}$ is an integer for every positive integer $n$, and determine for which $n$, $t$ divides $t_n$.

Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral, and $F$ the midpoint of arc $AB$ of its circumcircle not containing $C$ or $D$. Lines $DF$ and $AC$ meet at $P$; lines $CF$ and $BD$ meet at $Q$. Prove that $PQ$ is parallel to $AB$.
Determine all functions $f$ from the positive integers to the positive integers such that, whenever positive integers $a,b,c$ satisfy $1/a+1/b=1/c$, it follows that $1/f(a)+1/f(b)=1/f(c)$.

Anna buys one book every day and one shelf every alternate Thursday, starting Thursday 1 January 2015. On how many days between Thursday 1 January 2015 and Saturday 31 December 2016 inclusive is it possible for Anna to distribute all her books evenly (an equal number per shelf) across all her shelves?

Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral, with lines $CD$ and $BA$ meeting at $E$. The line through $D$ tangent to the circumcircle of $ADE$ meets line $CB$ at $F$. Prove that triangle $CDF$ is isosceles.

A sequence $t_0,t_1,t_2,\dots$ is given by $t_n = An^2+Bn+C$ for real constants $A\ne0$, $B$, $C$. Find values of $A,B,C$ maximizing the number of consecutive terms of this sequence that are also consecutive terms of the Fibonacci sequence ($F_0=0,F_1=1,F_m=F_{m-1}+F_{m-2}$).

James has a red jar, a blue jar, and 100 pebbles. A move transfers one pebble between the pile and a jar. At all times the red jar must contain at least as many pebbles as the blue jar, and the game must never revisit a previous state (given by the pebble counts in each jar). What is the maximum number of moves James can make?

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with feet of altitudes $D,E,F$ from $A,B,C$ respectively. Let $P,Q,R,S$ be the feet of the perpendiculars from $D$ to $BA,BE,CF,CA$ respectively. Prove that $P,Q,R,S$ are collinear.
A positive integer is called charming if it equals 2 or has the form $3^i5^j$ for non-negative integers $i,j$. Prove that every positive integer is a sum of distinct charming integers.
The integers $1,2,\dots,2016$ are each written in base 10 exactly once. How many of all the digits appearing across the whole list are odd?
For positive real $x$, let $\{x\}$ denote the greater of $x$ and $1/x$ (with $\{1\}=1$). Find, with proof, all positive real $y$ such that $5y\{8y\}\{25y\} = 1$.
Determine all pairs $(m,n)$ of positive integers satisfying $n^2-6n = m^2+m-10$.

Naomi and Tom alternately pick distinct integers from 1 to 100, Naomi first. A player loses if, after their move, the sum of all integers chosen so far cannot be written as a difference of two squares. Determine whether either player has a winning strategy, and if so, which.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with angle $A$ < angle $B$ < $90^\circ$, circumcircle $\Gamma$. The tangents to $\Gamma$ at $A$ and $C$ meet at $P$. Lines $AB$ and $PC$, extended, meet at $Q$. Given that the areas of triangles $ACP$, $ABC$, $BQC$ are all equal, prove that angle $BCA = 90^\circ$.
Consecutive integers $m,m+1,m+2,m+3$ are divisible respectively by consecutive odd integers $n,n+2,n+4,n+6$. Determine the smallest possible $m$ in terms of $n$.

Helen divides 365 in turn by each of $1,2,\dots,365$, listing the 365 remainders; Phil divides 366 in turn by each of $1,2,\dots,366$, listing the 366 remainders. Whose list of remainders has the greater sum, and by how much?
Over a 100-day period, each of six friends swims on exactly 75 days. Let $n$ be the number of days on which at least five of the friends swim. Find the largest and smallest possible values of $n$.

Triangle $ABC$ has $AB=CA$ and $BC$ as its longest side. Point $N$ on $BC$ satisfies $BN=AB$, and the line through $N$ perpendicular to $AB$ meets $AB$ at $M$. Prove that line $MN$ divides both the area and the perimeter of triangle $ABC$ into two equal parts.
A sequence of positive reals $a_1,a_2,\dots$ satisfies $a_1=1$ and $a_{n+1}+a_n = (a_{n+1}-a_n)^2$ for every $n\ge1$. How many possible values can $a_{2017}$ take?

A 100-comb is formed from a $2\times100$ grid by removing alternate squares from a long side, leaving 150 squares. In a $200\times200$ grid, $k$ squares are coloured so that no 150 uncoloured squares form a 100-comb. Find the smallest possible $k$.

Matthew has 300 cards numbered 1 to 300. He places cards one at a time in a row (each new card at the right end) so that at every stage the mean of the numbers in the row is an integer, stopping when no remaining card allows this. What is the smallest possible number of cards in the row when he stops? Give an example.

Five two-digit positive integers are written in increasing order on a blackboard, each a multiple of 3, using each of the digits $0$-$9$ exactly once across all five numbers (no leading zero). In how many ways can this be done?

For $n\ge3$, an $n$-ring is a circular arrangement of $n$ positive integers (not necessarily distinct) such that the product of every three consecutive integers equals $n$. How many integers $n$ with $3\le n\le 2018$ admit an $n$-ring?
Ares multiplies two integers differing by 9; Grace multiplies two integers differing by 6; both obtain the same product $T$. Determine all possible values of $T$.

Let $\Gamma$ be a semicircle with diameter $AB$, $C$ a point on $AB$, and $D,E$ points on arc $BA$ with $E$ between $B$ and $D$. Tangents to $\Gamma$ at $D$ and $E$ meet at $F$. Given angle $ACD$ = angle $ECB$, prove that angle $EFD$ = angle $ACD$ + angle $ECB$.
Two mathematically similar solid cylinders have heights summing to 1, surface areas summing to $8\pi$, and volumes summing to $2\pi$. Find all possible dimensions of each cylinder.

An ant starts at point $O$ and each minute walks 1 metre North, South, East, or West, returning to $O$ after 2018 minutes. If $n$ is the number of possible such journeys, find the highest power of 10 dividing $n$.

Show that there are at least three prime numbers $p$ less than 200 for which $p+2$, $p+6$, $p+8$ and $p+12$ are all prime. Show also that there is only one prime number $q$ for which $q+2$, $q+6$, $q+8$, $q+12$ and $q+14$ are all prime.
A sequence of integers $a_1, a_2, a_3, \dots$ satisfies the relation $4a_{n+1}^2 - 4a_na_{n+1} + a_n^2 - 1 = 0$ for all positive integers $n$. What are the possible values of $a_1$?

Two circles $S_1$ and $S_2$ are tangent at $P$. A common tangent, not through $P$, touches $S_1$ at $A$ and $S_2$ at $B$. Points $C$ and $D$, on $S_1$ and $S_2$ respectively, are outside the triangle $APB$ and are such that $P$ is on the line $CD$. Prove that $AC$ is perpendicular to $BD$.

There are 2019 penguins waddling towards their favourite restaurant. As the penguins arrive, they are handed tickets numbered in ascending order from 1 to 2019, and told to join the queue. The first penguin starts the queue. For each $n > 1$ the penguin holding ticket number $n$ finds the greatest $m < n$ which divides $n$ and enters the queue directly behind the penguin holding ticket number $m$. This continues until all 2019 penguins are in the queue. (a) How many penguins are in front of the penguin with ticket number 2? (b) What numbers are on the tickets held by the penguins just in front of and just behind the penguin holding ticket 33?

Six children are evenly spaced around a circular table. Initially, one has a pile of $n > 0$ sweets in front of them, and the others have nothing. If a child has at least four sweets in front of them, they may perform the following move: eat one sweet and give one sweet to each of their immediate neighbours and to the child directly opposite them. An arrangement is called perfect if there is a sequence of moves which results in each child having the same number of sweets in front of them. For which values of $n$ is the initial arrangement perfect?

A function $f$ is called good if it assigns an integer value $f(m,n)$ to every ordered pair of integers $(m,n)$ in such a way that for every pair of integers $(m,n)$ we have $$2f(m,n) = f(m-n,\, n-m) + m + n = f(m+1,\, n) + f(m,\, n+1) - 1.$$ Find all good functions.

[Section A — answer only] Alice and Bob take it in turns to write numbers on a blackboard. Alice starts by writing an integer $a$ between $-100$ and $100$ inclusive on the board. On each of Bob's turns he writes twice the number Alice wrote last. On each of Alice's subsequent turns she writes the number 45 less than the number Bob wrote last. At some point, the number $a$ is written on the board for a second time. Find the possible values of $a$.

[Section A — answer only] A triangle has side lengths $a$, $a$ and $b$. It has perimeter $P$ and area $A$. Given that $b$ and $P$ are integers, and that $P$ is numerically equal to $A^2$, find all possible pairs $(a,b)$.

[Section A — answer only] A square piece of paper is folded in half along a line of symmetry. The resulting shape is then folded in half along a line of symmetry of the new shape. This process is repeated until $n$ folds have been made, giving a sequence of $n+1$ shapes. If we do not distinguish between congruent shapes, find the number of possible sequences when (a) $n=3$; (b) $n=6$; (c) $n=9$. (When $n=1$ there are two possible sequences.)

[Section A — answer only] In the equation $$\mathrm{A}^{\mathrm{AA}} + \mathrm{AA} = \mathrm{B,BBC,DED,BEE,BBB,BBE}$$ the letters A, B, C, D and E represent different base 10 digits (so the right hand side is a sixteen digit number and AA is a two digit number). Given that $\mathrm{C} = 9$, find A, B, D and E.

[Section B] Let points $A$, $B$ and $C$ lie on a circle $\Gamma$. Circle $\Delta$ is tangent to $AC$ at $A$. It meets $\Gamma$ again at $D$ and the line $AB$ again at $P$. The point $A$ lies between points $B$ and $P$. Prove that if $AD = DP$, then $BP = AC$.

[Section B] Given that an integer $n$ is the sum of two different powers of 2 and also the sum of two different Mersenne primes, prove that $n$ is the sum of two different square numbers. (A Mersenne prime is a prime number which is one less than a power of two.)

[Section B] Evie and Odette are playing a game. Three pebbles are placed on the number line; one at $-2020$, one at $2020$, and one at $n$, where $n$ is an integer between $-2020$ and $2020$. They take it in turns moving either the leftmost or the rightmost pebble to an integer between the other two pebbles. The game ends when the pebbles occupy three consecutive integers. Odette wins if their sum is odd; Evie wins if their sum is even. For how many values of $n$ can Evie guarantee victory if (a) Odette goes first; (b) Evie goes first?

Find three even numbers less than 400, each of which can be expressed as a sum of consecutive positive odd numbers in at least six different ways. (Two expressions are considered to be different if they contain different numbers. The order of the numbers forming a sum is irrelevant.)

One day Arun and Disha played several games of table tennis. At five points during the day, Arun calculated the percentage of the games played so far that he had won. The results of these calculations were exactly 30%, exactly 40%, exactly 50%, exactly 60% and exactly 70% in some order. What is the smallest possible number of games they played?

For each integer $0 \le n \le 11$, Eliza has exactly three identical pieces of gold that weigh $2^n$ grams. In how many different ways can she form a pile of gold weighing 2021 grams? (Two piles are different if they contain different numbers of gold pieces of some weight. The arrangement of the pieces in the piles is irrelevant.)

Two circles $\Gamma_1$ and $\Gamma_2$ have centres $O_1$ and $O_2$ respectively. They pass through each other's centres and intersect at $A$ and $B$. The point $C$ lies on the minor arc $BO_2$ of $\Gamma_1$. The points $D$ and $E$ lie on the line $O_2C$ such that $\angle AO_1D = \angle DO_1C$ and $\angle CO_1E = \angle EO_1B$. Prove that triangle $DO_1E$ is equilateral. (A minor arc of a circle is the shorter of the two arcs with given endpoints.)

An $N$-set is a set of different positive integers including a given positive integer $N$. Let $m(N)$ be the smallest possible mean of any $N$-set. For how many values of $N$ less than 2021 is $m(N)$ an integer?

Marvin has been tasked with writing down every list of integers with the following properties: (i) the list contains 71 terms; (ii) the first term is 1; (iii) every term after the first is equal to either the previous term, or the sum of all previous terms. When Marvin is finished, how many of the lists will have a sum equal to 999,999?

A road has houses numbered from 1 to $n$, where $n$ is a three-digit number. Exactly $\frac{1}{k}$ of the numbers start with the digit 2, where $k$ is a positive integer. Find the possible values of $n$.

A sequence of positive integers $a_n$ begins with $a_1 = a$ and $a_2 = b$ for positive integers $a$ and $b$. Subsequent terms in the sequence satisfy the following two rules for all positive integers $n$: $$a_{2n+1} = a_{2n}a_{2n-1}, \qquad a_{2n+2} = a_{2n+1} + 4.$$ Exactly $m$ of the numbers $a_1, a_2, a_3, \dots, a_{2022}$ are square numbers. What is the maximum possible value of $m$? Note that $m$ depends on $a$ and $b$, so the maximum is over all possible choices of $a$ and $b$.

In an acute, non-isosceles triangle $ABC$ the midpoints of $AC$ and $AB$ are $B_1$ and $C_1$ respectively. A point $D$ lies on $BC$ with $C$ between $B$ and $D$. The point $F$ is such that $\angle AFC$ is a right angle and $\angle DCF = \angle FCA$. The point $G$ is such that $\angle AGB$ is a right angle and $\angle CBG = \angle GBA$. Prove that $B_1$, $C_1$, $F$ and $G$ are collinear.

Alex and Katy play a game on an $8 \times 8$ square grid made of 64 unit cells. They take it in turns to play, with Alex going first. On Alex's turn, he writes 'A' in an empty cell. On Katy's turn, she writes 'K' in two empty cells that share an edge. The game ends when one player cannot move. Katy's score is the number of Ks on the grid at the end of the game. What is the highest score Katy can be sure to get if she plays well, no matter what Alex does?

For each integer $n \ge 1$, let $f(n)$ be the number of lists of different positive integers starting with 1 and ending with $n$, in which each term except the last divides its successor. Prove that for each integer $N \ge 1$ there is an integer $n \ge 1$ such that $N$ divides $f(n)$. (So $f(1)=1$, $f(2)=1$ and $f(6)=3$.)

A circle $\Gamma$ has radius 1. A line $l$ is such that the perpendicular distance from $l$ to the centre of $\Gamma$ is strictly between 0 and 2. A frog chooses a point on $\Gamma$ whose perpendicular distance from $l$ is less than 1 and sits on that point. It then performs a sequence of jumps. Each jump has length 1 and if a jump starts on $\Gamma$ it must end on $l$ and vice versa. Prove that after some finite number of jumps the frog returns to a point it has been on before.

An unreliable typist can guarantee that when they try to type a word with different letters, every letter of the word will appear exactly once in what they type, and each letter will occur at most one letter late (though it may occur more than one letter early). Thus, when trying to type MATHS, the typist may type MATHS, MTAHS or TMASH, but not ATMSH. Determine, with proof, the number of possible spellings of OLYMPIADS that might be typed.

The sequence of integers $a_0, a_1, \dots$ has the property that for each $i \ge 2$, $a_i$ is either $2a_{i-1} - a_{i-2}$ or $2a_{i-2} - a_{i-1}$. Given that $a_{2023}$ and $a_{2024}$ are consecutive integers, prove that $a_0$ and $a_1$ are consecutive integers. (Note that 6 and 7 are consecutive integers, as are 7 and 6.)

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $\angle ACB < \angle BAC < 90^\circ$. Let $X$ and $Y$ be points on $AC$ and the circle $ABC$ respectively such that $X, Y \ne A$ and $BX = BY = BA$. Line $XY$ intersects the circle $ABC$ again at $Z$. Prove that $BZ$ is perpendicular to $AC$.
Find all positive integers $n$ such that $n \times 2^n + 1$ is a square.

An artist arranges 1000 dots evenly around a circle, with each dot being either red or blue. A critic looks at the artwork and counts faults: each time two red dots are adjacent is one fault, and each time two blue dots are exactly two apart (that is, they have exactly one dot in between them) is another. What is the smallest number of faults the critic could find?

For some integer $n > 4$ a convex polygon has vertices $v_1, v_2, \dots, v_n$ in that cyclic order. All its edges are the same length. It also has the property that the lengths of the diagonals $v_1v_4, v_2v_5, \dots, v_{n-3}v_n, v_{n-2}v_1, v_{n-1}v_2$ and $v_nv_3$ are all equal. For which $n$ is it necessarily the case that the polygon has equal angles?

We say that the positive integer $n \ge 3$ is happy if it is possible to arrange $n$ different positive integers in a circle such that two conditions are satisfied: (a) if integers $u$ and $v$ in the circle are neighbours, then either $u$ divides $v$ or $v$ divides $u$; (b) if different integers $u$ and $v$ are in the circle but are not neighbours, then neither divides the other. Determine, with proof, which positive integers $n$ in the range $3 \le n \le 12$ are happy.

A magician performs a trick with a deck of $n$ cards that are numbered from 1 to $n$. The magician prepares for the trick by putting the cards in an order of her choosing. Then she challenges a member of the audience to write an integer on a board. The magician turns over the cards one by one, in their pre-arranged order. Every time the magician turns over a card, the audience member multiplies the number on the board by $-1$, adds it to the number on the card, writes the result on the board, and erases the old number. The magician guarantees that, no matter which initial integer is chosen, the initial and final numbers will sum to 0. Determine for which natural numbers $n$ the magician can perform the trick. You must both prove that the trick is possible for the numbers you claim, and prove that it is not possible for any other numbers.

Rhian and Jack are playing a game in which initially the number $10^6$ is written on a blackboard. If the current number on the board is $n$, a move consists of choosing two different positive integers $a, b$ such that $n = ab$ and replacing $n$ with $|a-b|$. Rhian starts, then the players make moves alternately. A player loses if they are unable to move. Determine, with proof, which player has a winning strategy.

In the acute-angled triangle $ABC$ we have $AB < AC < BC$. The midpoint of $BC$ is $M$. There is a point $P$ on the line segment $AM$ such that $AB = CP$, and $\angle PAB = \angle BCP$. Prove that $\angle CPB = 90^\circ$.

Let $p$ be a prime number, and let $n$ be the smallest positive integer, strictly greater than 1, for which $n^6 - 1$ is divisible by $p$. Prove that at least one of $(n+1)^6 - 1$ and $(n+2)^6 - 1$ is divisible by $p$.

Björk has 64 sugar cubes, all of size $1 \times 1 \times 1$. Each sugar cube is either white or demerara or muscovado in flavour. She piles the sugar cubes into a neat $4 \times 4 \times 4$ cube. Prove that there must be 12 sugar cubes of the same flavour which can be put into 6 disjoint pairs so that the distance between the centres of the cubes in each pair is the same.

A ramp is a sequence of three different positive integers $a, b, c$ such that $a$ is a factor of $b$ and $b$ is a factor of $c$. For every prime number $p$ and every positive integer $n$, determine with proof whether $p^n$ can be expressed as the sum of a ramp.
Find all triples $(x, y, z)$ of real numbers satisfying the equations $$x^2 + 2yz = 4, \qquad y^2 + 2zx = 4, \qquad z^2 + 2xy = 1.$$

An $11 \times 11$ square grid is dissected into 11 pieces as follows. At each step, remove the top row and the leftmost column of the remaining grid as a single piece. Thus, the pieces obtained are L-shaped with sizes $21, 19, \dots, 3$, together with a single square. The pieces are rearranged to reassemble an $11 \times 11$ grid, with rotations allowed (but the pieces may not be turned over) so that the single square occupies the cell in the third row and third column (counting from the top left). How many ways can this be done?

Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with $AB > AC$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$. The circle passing through $M$ that is tangent to $AB$ at $B$ and the circle passing through $M$ that is tangent to $AC$ at $C$ intersect again at $D$. Prove that $MA \times MD = MB \times MC$.

George defines a sequence of positive integers $t_1, t_2, t_3, \dots$ as follows. He first sets $t_1 = 1$. Then, for $n \ge 1$: if $t_n$ is even, then $t_{n+1} = t_n/2$; if $t_n$ is odd and greater than 1, then $t_{n+1}$ is $t_n/3$ rounded to the nearest integer; if $t_n = 1$, then $t_{n+1} = 2025k$, where $k$ is the number of terms equal to 1 amongst $t_1, t_2, \dots, t_n$. Does this sequence contain every positive integer?

There are 1000 lily pads on a pond arranged in a circle and labelled $1, 2, \dots, 1000$ in order. (The first four lily pads may also be described using the labels 1001, 1002, 1003 and 1004, respectively.) The first $n$ lily pads are each occupied by a frog with the remaining lily pads not occupied. Each minute, exactly one of the frogs makes a move. Suppose the frog is on lily pad $k$. That frog may either (i) swim to lily pad $k+4$ or $k-4$, provided that it is not occupied; or (ii) jump to lily pad $k+3$ or $k-3$, provided that this lily pad is not occupied and the two lily pads jumped over are both occupied. When this happens, the two frogs that were jumped over dive into the pond and don't participate in any further moves. For which values of $n$ is it possible, by a sequence of moves, to end with exactly one frog remaining on the lily pads?
